question: A number of companies and stakeholders in the creative manufacturing industry have highlighted that AI uptake is being hampered by a lack of operational skills across the board, uncertainty about requirements, and difficulties in accessing the AI Act’s measures. In the EU, AI uptake among large companies (41 % in 2024) is significantly higher than among SMEs (13%).

Articles 57, 62 and 96 and recitals 143 and 145 of the AI Act provide for support measures for SMEs and start-ups which include the provision of priority access to sandboxes, dedicated training and standard templates, as well as compliance cost reductions, the single information platform and best practices for public procurement procedures.
Having regard for the requirements currently in force – which concern AI literacy (Article 4) and other matters – and the upcoming implementing measures: 1.

Could the Commission provide clarification as to the timeframe, format and content of the guidelines provided for in Article 96, specifically as regards the SMEs and sectors (including the creative manufacturing and cultural industries) that need the most help with AI?
What practical tools (short forms, minimum standards, examples for non-technical profiles) will be made available for manufacturing SMEs that have a strong creative component?

What actions will the Commission take in conjunction with the European AI Office and Member States to ensure that micro and small enterprises enjoy genuine access to European Digital Innovation Hubs and that the implementation of the measures referred to in Article 62 is monitored?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The guidelines on prohibited AI practices1 and on AI system definition2 were adopted in February 2025. The guidelines on the implementation of transparency obligations3 and on the classification of high-risk AI systems4 were opened for public consultation. Other guidelines listed in Article 96 of the AI Act5 are in preparation6.

Besides, the framework for AI regulatory sandboxes as set out in the AI Act and in forthcoming implementing acts, Member States are supported in the implementation of AI regulatory sandboxes through tools developed in the context of the AI Board.
These include templates (such as for the application form to access such sandboxes) and a guidebook that consider the specific needs and circumstances of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

Workforce of SMEs will also benefit from other EU-funded projects, such as the AI Skills Academy, which will support AI upskilling and reskilling in key sectors such as cultural and creative industries by promoting on-the-job training and by gathering AI courses per sector and job-profile.
The Commission underlines the important role of the European Digital Innovation Hubs (EDIHs) in supporting the digital transformation and AI uptake of micro, small and mediumsized enterprises.

As AI experience centres, EDIHs are expected to serve as first points of contact for businesses to provide initial support and practical guidance on the AI Act, and to link SMEs to other initiatives such as testing and experimentation facilities and AI factories.

The AI Office will, in cooperation with Member States, continue to support a coordinated approach to the implementation of the AI Act, including as regards AI regulatory sandboxes in the context of the AI Board and forthcoming implementing acts.
